title: Uber and Lyft Accident Lawyer Cost: Fees and Insurance by Period (2026)
description: What a rideshare accident lawyer charges, which Uber or Lyft policy applies in each app period, California's PUC 5433 minimums, and a worked example.
h1: How much does an Uber or Lyft accident lawyer cost?
summary: Rideshare accident lawyers usually charge a contingency fee, commonly quoted at one-third of the recovery and nothing if there is no recovery. The bigger cost factor is insurance: Uber and Lyft list at least $1 million in liability coverage during trips and pickups in most markets, but only $50,000/$100,000 for injuries and $25,000 for property while the app is on and waiting, and nothing from the company when the app is off. Limits vary by state; California law requires $60,000/$300,000 UM/UIM during rides.
body:
How rideshare accident lawyers charge

Lawyers who handle Uber and Lyft crash claims for injured passengers, drivers, pedestrians or other motorists almost always work on a contingency fee: a percentage of the recovery, nothing if there is no recovery. The agreement must be in a signed writing that states the percentage at each stage and whether case expenses are deducted before or after the fee.[1] One-third is the most commonly quoted starting point and is the legal maximum for injury cases in Michigan;[2] Florida presumes fees above 33⅓% (before an answer) or 40% (after an answer) of the first $1 million excessive,[3] and Connecticut uses a sliding scale.[4]

What makes rideshare cases different is not the fee but the insurance: which policy applies depends on what the driver's app was doing at the moment of the crash. Sorting that out is a large part of the lawyer's work and can decide whether there is meaningful coverage at all.

Which insurance applies: the three app periods

Uber and Lyft both describe coverage in periods. The figures below are what each company publishes for most U.S. markets as of October 2026; both say coverage varies by state.[5][6]

Uber and Lyft third-party liability coverage by period (most markets)
PeriodUberLyft
App off (personal driving)Driver's personal auto policy only[5]Driver's personal auto policy only[6]
App on, waiting for a request$50,000 per person and $100,000 per accident for injuries; $25,000 property damage[5]$50,000 per person and $100,000 per accident bodily injury; $25,000 property damage, when personal insurance does not apply[6]
En route to pick up, and during the tripAt least $1,000,000 for injuries and property damage[5]At least $1,000,000 third-party liability in most markets[6]

Both companies say uninsured/underinsured motorist (UM/UIM), personal injury protection and medical payments coverage depend on state law and are not available everywhere.[5][6] Lyft lists exceptions: in Arizona and Nebraska its waiting-period limits follow state minimums ($25,000/$50,000 bodily injury, $20,000 property damage); en route limits are a $125,000 combined single limit in Maryland and $250,000 in Arizona; and it does not procure insurance for NYC TLC drivers, certain New York counties, or livery drivers nationwide.[6] Uber points drivers to the certificates of insurance for their state.[5]

California example: Public Utilities Code 5433

Some states write minimums into law. California's code (2025 edition, as amended by SB 371) requires, from acceptance of a ride until it is complete, $1,000,000 primary coverage for death, personal injury and property damage, and TNC-provided UM/UIM of $60,000 per person and $300,000 per incident from when a passenger enters the vehicle until they exit.[7] While a driver is logged on but not on a ride, it requires $50,000 per person and $100,000 per incident for death and injury, $30,000 for property damage, and $200,000 per occurrence in excess coverage.[7] The amendment is shown as effective January 1, 2026.[7]

Coverage figures change. Before relying on any number here, ask the lawyer to confirm the policy in force on the crash date for your state; Uber's own page says limits "vary by state and have changed over time."[5]

Why your role in the crash matters

  • Passenger: you were in the trip period, so the $1 million-level liability coverage generally applies if the rideshare driver was at fault; if another driver was at fault, that driver's insurer comes first and the rideshare policy's UM/UIM may apply where it exists.
  • Other driver or pedestrian: the period matters most. A crash while the app was off may leave only the driver's personal policy, which may exclude commercial use.
  • Rideshare driver: a driver's own injuries are handled differently from a passenger's, and what is available depends on the state and the app period. Some states add coverage: Uber lists occupational accident coverage in California and Massachusetts and workers' compensation coverage in Washington in some periods.[5]

Evidence that saves cost later

  • Screenshot the trip in your app (trip ID, time, route, driver name, vehicle) and keep receipts and in-app messages.
  • Get the police report number, photos and witness names.
  • Report the crash in the app, but keep statements factual and short; let a lawyer handle recorded statements.
  • Ask your lawyer to request the company's app data showing the driver's status at the moment of the crash. That data decides which period, and which policy, applies.

Worked example: why the period changes your net

Illustrative example only. A pedestrian's damages are documented at $150,000, and the fee is one-third of the gross, with $8,000 in costs.

App on, waiting: the company policy listed above pays at most $50,000 per person for injuries. Fee $50,000 × 1/3 ≈ $16,667. Net before liens: $50,000 − $16,667 − $8,000 ≈ $25,333, unless other coverage (your own UM/UIM, other at-fault parties) is found.

Trip in progress: the $1,000,000 liability coverage is not the limiting factor. If the claim resolves at $150,000: fee $50,000; net before liens $150,000 − $50,000 − $8,000 = $92,000.

When available coverage is small, ask whether the firm will reduce its percentage so that you are not left with a few thousand dollars after liens. Lien rules and a full net-recovery example are on the personal injury lawyer cost page.

Questions to ask before you sign

  • Which policy do you expect to apply, and how will you prove the driver's app status?
  • Does the fee apply to my own UM/UIM, med-pay or PIP claim, and at what rate?
  • Is the fee calculated on the gross or after costs, and do I owe costs if we lose?[1]
  • If coverage is limited, will you reduce the percentage?
  • What is my filing deadline? See the general deadline on your state page.

faq.q: Who pays if my Uber or Lyft driver caused the crash?
faq.a: If the driver was on a trip or en route to you, the company's commercial policy (at least $1 million liability in most markets, per Uber and Lyft) generally applies. If the app was off, only the driver's personal policy applies, and limits are lower while the app is on but waiting for a request.

faq.q: Do rideshare accident lawyers charge more than other injury lawyers?
faq.a: Usually not; the percentage is typically the same contingency fee used for car crashes. The extra work is in getting the app-status data and identifying the right policy.

faq.q: Does Uber or Lyft cover uninsured drivers who hit me as a passenger?
faq.a: Only where the company carries UM/UIM, which both say varies by state. California law requires $60,000 per person and $300,000 per incident of UM/UIM while a passenger is in the vehicle.

faq.q: Can a rideshare driver get workers' compensation?
faq.a: It depends on the state. Uber lists workers' compensation in Washington and occupational accident coverage in California and Massachusetts for certain periods.
